Aqaba Marine Reserve (AMR) is Jordan’s first marine protected area extending over approximately 7 kilometres (in length) representing 27% of the total length of the Jordanian coastline and a total area of 2.8 sq km (before counting the surrounding buffer zone). The reserve’s terrestrial boundary lies 50 meters east of the Mean High-Water Mark (MHWM), while the marine boundary extends 350 meters west of the MHWM. AMR is home to a diverse coral reef system known for its high-latitude reef formations, which include two key morphological reef units: the coral reef flat and the outer reef slope. The Gulf of Aqaba contains 157 hard coral species composed of 153 scleractinian corals, one organ pipe coral, and 3 fire corals. Among these, 15 endemic species of the Red Sea were recorded within AMR. The terrestrial ecosystem is less rich, but the area was declared as an IBA with 250 different species, and up to 1.5 million birds flying over it. Despite global environmental challenges, the coral reefs in the AMR have demonstrated significant climate resilience, showing no major effects from bleaching, thanks to the unique conditions of the Gulf of Aqaba, which buffer the area from high waves, strong currents, and potential seismic events like tsunamis, in addition to the effective conservation efforts that date back to 1997. Key Achievements Conservation The tools of protection and enforcement applied within the AMR resulted in conservation of the natural values, and this is proved by the results of the monitoring programs such as the national monitoring program. Effective surveillance and patrolling are being implementing to cover the entire AMR area, including hiring of 8 new staff as beach rangers. Creating artificial reefs and diving sites to relieve pressure on natural coral reefs. Installation of mooring buoys for use by diving boats and pleasure boats, for the purpose of regulating the mooring and alignment of these boats, and avoiding the dropping of anchors on coral reefs and bottom habitats; Good governance AMR has a clear governance structure described in “The Aqaba Marine Reserve Bylaw” which was issued in 2022, the bylaw was prepared and approved after several meetings with the stakeholders and representative from local community. The bylaw clearly describes the Geographic Boundaries of the AMR and its buffer Zone, The advisory committee of the AMR (It’s membership and roles and responsibilities), The management authority, financial mechanisms, land use, and the restricted/ Forbidden activities within the site. Consultation with local communities and engagement of the related stakeholders with regards to important decisions need to be taken by the site management. Women participation has been encouraged by hiring four females out of eight new staff, they are taking a vital role in different departments in the AMR. Community benefits AMR has provided several job opportunities for local community. Improve the beach facilities and services for the site visitors. The protection of natural values such as coral reef and seagrass ecosystems has contributed to income increase of different local community sectors such as diving centers and glass boat owners. The reserve’s terrestrial boundary lies 50 meters east of the Mean High-Water Mark (MHWM), while the marine boundary extends 350 meters west of the MHWM. The AMR was established and managed as a Marine Park during the period (1997- Dec. 2020) with clear governance arrangements, institutional arrangements and an active and periodically updated management and zoning plans. Active programmes included the conservation of the coral reefs and fish as key natural values for establishing the park, patrolling and surveillance programme, environmental awareness and a monitoring programme. It was declared as a Marine Reserve in 2020 to enhance and continue the conservation efforts that started in 1997, in alignment with the National Protected Areas bylaws that govern the network of PAs in the country. 1. The fish community. 1. coral percentage coverage. 2. water quality within different locations under different indicators. 3. average number of fish species per 250 sqm. 1.The coral reefs in the AMR are amongst the most diverse per square meter in the world, including 157 identified hard coral species and 120 species of soft coral, some of which are considered vulnerable and some are classified as near threatened according to IUCN. According to several studies, it has been proven that the Aqaba coral reef is uniquely resilient to global warming and climate change. 2.The water quality in the Aqaba Marine Reserve is maintained through the reserve's regulating ecosystem services, specifically shoreline protection, carbon reservoir and climate regulation, and water filtration, which collectively contribute to the preservation and enhancement of water quality. 3.The Gulf of Aqaba harbours around 515 marine fish species, of which 507 species belong to 109 families have been recorded in the AMR. The rate of endemism is considered high and represents 13.7% of the total fish species recorded, with seven fish species recognized as endemic to the Gulf of Aqaba The results of different monitoring programs have shown stability of the natural values, which means efficient protection. 2. AMR is adopting the number of visitors as a success measure for the protection of cultural values; therefore, we monitor the number of visitors to the AMR in three ways: 1. The number of divers on the diving sites 2. The number of visitors participating in the educational and environmental awareness activities conducted by the AMR team 3.The number of visitors to Aqaba city in general is also considered as good indication of status of the cultural values. Based on the number of visitors as mentioned above during the last five years, the cultural values protected by the AMR is considered good and being protected. The outcome results show stability with regards to cultural values. Conservation Summary MEWA EAGL recommends adding Aqaba Marine Reserve (AMR) to the IUCN Green List as it demonstrates overall strong alignment with the IUCN Green List Standard. AMR was established in 2020, however, its conservation history dates back to 1997 when it was established as a marine park with a dedicated governing bylaws, active management plan, active patrolling, awareness and monitoring programmes. With the commitment and support of King Abdullah II, who considers it to be an outstanding national priority, the site was designated as a marine reserve in 2020, following a participatory process and with a new bylaw and a new management plan that fulfils the requirements of the new designation and aligns with its management category. The Aqaba Special Economic Zone Authority (ASEZA) was appointed as its management authority. In addition to the political support, ASEZA adopted a participatory approach engaging all stakeholders in key issues related to AMR, like zoning, management of tourism activities, fishing regulations, etc. Partnerships were developed with entities, like the navy, environmental police, marine science station, development agencies, private sector, hotels, and CBO’s. Conservation: Monitoring reports provided by the marine science station demonstrate that AMR , and (previously Aqaba Marine Park AMP) is succeeding to conserve the globally significant marine ecosystem, and one of the world’s most resilient coral reef systems with stable and positive trends and successful coral rehabilitation programmes. The site is recommended for the Green List with the following recommendations to be achieved by the Green List mid-term review: Recommendation 1: It is recommended that the site conducts an economic valuation of the ecosystem services provided (terrestrial – marine) to link the economic values with the identified thresholds and support management decisions. Recommendation 2: To conduct a carrying capacity study for the diving sites to be used to take the necessary actions needed and to support in establishing thresholds for the ecosystem services.
